description: CrewPulse is a web app that lets astronauts assess their own health during a mission and tells them what to do next. A two-minute daily check-in (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise, vision symptoms and dosimeter reading) feeds a clickable body map coloured green, amber or red. Each area explains why spaceflight affects it, using NASA's Human Research Program hazards, and gives step-by-step actions.
summary: CrewPulse is a web app that lets astronauts assess their own health during a mission and tells them what to do next. A two-minute daily check-in (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise, vision symptoms and dosimeter reading) feeds a clickable body map coloured green, amber or red. Each area explains why spaceflight affects it, using NASA's Human Research Program hazards, and gives step-by-step actions. Its key idea is to compare every reading with the astronaut's own baseline as well as with population ranges. We tested that idea on real Inspiration4 crew blood panels from NASA's Open Science Data Repository. On the day after landing, 25 lab values moved more than 2 spreads from each crew member's pre-flight baseline, and 18 of them (72%) were still inside the normal lab range, so a range-only check would miss them. Guidance also adapts to the environment: on the Moon the crew can call the ground, while in Mars transit, where replies take minutes, CrewPulse tells them to start the on-board protocol first.
details:
What it does

CrewPulse is a visual self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where they carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in their own health.

·       Daily check-in: eleven indicators an astronaut can measure on board (resting heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, temperature, SpO2, fasting glucose, sleep hours, mood, exercise minutes, vision change or headache, cumulative radiation dose). Each input shows a live status dot.

·       Body map: eight clickable areas (brain and behaviour, eyes, heart and circulation, lungs and oxygen, immune system, metabolism and kidneys, bones and muscles, radiation dose), each coloured by its worst indicator.

·       Explanations and actions: for every indicator the panel says what the value means, why spaceflight affects it (linked to the NASA HRP hazard), what to do now, and when to escalate. Every threshold shows its source.

·       Personal baseline: from mission day 8, each reading is also compared with the astronaut's own days 1 to 7. A value that is normal for the population but more than 2 spreads away from the astronaut's own normal turns amber.

·       Environment awareness: space station, lunar base, Mars transit and Mars base presets change the signal delay, gravity and daily radiation rate. Red findings in Mars transit or on Mars produce 'start the on-board protocol now, send the report after' instead of 'call the flight surgeon'.

·       Trends: a mission timeline for any indicator with the population band, the personal band and coloured alert points.

·       Real crew data: an explorer for the Inspiration4 complete blood count and metabolic panel (NASA OSDR OSD-569 and OSD-575), four crew, seven time points, with each person's lab range and personal pre-flight band.

·       Gamification: a mission routine checklist, a countermeasure streak and mission health points that reward exercise and sleep.

What we found in NASA data

We applied CrewPulse's personal-baseline rule to the Inspiration4 panels. Baseline = mean of the three pre-flight draws (L-92, L-44, L-3); spread = the larger of their standard deviation and 5% of the mean (a stated floor, because three draws underestimate variability). On the day after return (R+1), 146 crew-analyte pairs could be tested. 25 moved more than 2 spreads from the person's own baseline, and 18 of those 25 (72%) were still inside the laboratory reference range. Example: crew member C003's white blood cell count fell from a 9.6 thousand/uL baseline to 7.0, 5.4 spreads lower, while the lab range (3.8 to 10.8) calls it normal. This is a small, short mission (4 people, 3 days), so we present it as an illustration of why personal baselines matter, not as clinical validation.

How it works

·       scripts/build_dataset.py downloads both OSDR tables, averages duplicate draws, computes baselines, spreads and z-scores for every crew member and analyte, and writes data/i4_labs.json and js/data.js.

·       js/domains.js holds the knowledge base: environments with signal delay, gravity and published daily dose rates (Moon 1.369 mSv/day, Zhang et al. 2020; Mars cruise 1.84 mSv/day, Zeitlin et al. 2013; Mars surface 0.64 mSv/day, Hassler et al. 2014), indicator thresholds (AHA blood pressure and heart rate, ADA glucose, AASM/SRS sleep, NASA 600 mSv career limit, NASA exercise and bone-loss figures), body regions and action lists.

·       js/sim.js generates a seeded, labelled 30-day mission log (stable first two weeks, then sleep debt, falling mood, rising resting heart rate and missed exercise) so judges can explore without entering data.

·       js/app.js applies two checks per reading (population rule and personal z-score), takes the worse one, and renders the body map, panels and SVG charts. Every state is in the URL, so any view can be shared.

·       Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no libraries and no server; it runs on GitHub Pages, offline, or on a tablet on board.

Benefits

·       Astronauts get a quick, understandable picture of their health and clear next steps, without needing medical training.

·       Personal baselines catch slow drifts that population ranges hide, which matters on missions too long and too far for routine ground review.

·       Advice that respects signal delay supports crew autonomy on Mars missions.

·       On Earth, the same approach suits remote workers, polar stations and patients managing chronic conditions at home.

What we hope to achieve

Next steps: connect wearable sensors, let flight surgeons tune thresholds per astronaut, and test the personal-baseline rule on longer-duration NASA datasets such as the Twins Study.

Tools

JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG; Python 3 (standard library); NASA OSDR public file API; GitHub Pages; Playwright and ffmpeg for the demo video; Kokoro TTS for narration.
